notes: serpens: i-stem, genitive plural serpentium; the noun is the present participle of serpo used as a noun
vox: genitive plural vocum, and the stem voc- shows only from the genitive on
pectus: genitive plural pectorum, neuter plural pectora
perizoma: a Greek neuter in -ma, so the stem is perizomat- — genitive plural perizomatum, neuter plural perizomata
dolor: genitive plural dolorum
labor: genitive plural laborum
sudor: genitive plural sudorum
potestas: genitive plural potestatum
panis: genitive plural panum, not panium
pulvis: genitive plural pulverum, and the stem pulver- shows only from the genitive on
caput: genitive plural capitum, neuter plural capita
mater: genitive plural matrum, not materum
ficus, ficus, f.: fourth declension and feminine, like most tree names; it is also declined ficus, fici (second declension)
Heva, Hevæ, f. declines as a first-declension noun (Hevam in 4:1); the form Heva in 3:20 is the nominative quoted as a name, not an indeclinable
Adam is indeclinable in the nominative, accusative and ablative, but takes a first-declension dative and genitive Adæ (3:17, 3:21)
cherubim: a Hebrew plural taken into Latin unchanged; it is indeclinable and already plural
ambo, ambæ, ambo: plural by nature like duo, with the -o nominative and -obus/-abus dative and ablative
callidior, callidius is the comparative of callidus; superlative callidissimus
vester, vestra, vestrum: the stem is vestr-, so there is no e in vestri or vestrorum
æternus, æterna, æternum: in æternum is the neuter used as a noun, 'for ever'
quis, quid: the interrogative has two terminations and no separate feminine
tui in 3:19 is tuus (genitive of your face), but tui in 3:16 is the genitive of tu, governed by dominabitur — one form, two words
tango, tangere, tetigi, tactus: the perfect tetigi is reduplicated and drops the n of the present stem
pario, parere, peperi, partus: the perfect peperi is reduplicated, and the present stem is pari- (paries, pariam)
contero, conterere, contrivi, contritus: the perfect and supine shorten the stem to contri-
consuo, consuere, consui, consutus: a compound of suo (to sew), not of sum
timeo, timere, timui: no supine in use
abscondit is both the present and the perfect third singular of abscondo; only the context separates them
comedit is both the present and the perfect third singular of comedo; in 3:6 both occurrences are perfect
vesceris is both the present and the future second singular of vescor; the donec clause makes 3:19 future
audisti and audissent are syncopated for audivisti and audivissent
revertor, reverti, reversus sum: deponent in the present system, but its perfect reverti is active in form
gradior, gradi, gressus sum: deponent, and the supine stem gress- shares nothing with the present grad-
scio, scire, scivi, scitus: the imperative is scito, not sci
maledico, maledicere, maledixi, maledictus: a compound of dico, so the imperative is maledic, not maledice
maledicta in 3:17 is the perfect participle standing as a predicate with est left out
custodiendam in 3:24 is the gerundive agreeing with viam, not the gerund; the build tables it with the gerund
cum is a conjunction here (cum audissent, cumque cognovissent) and a preposition elsewhere: one surface form, two words
dii is the plural of Deus, used of false gods in 3:5; the singular keeps its capital in this text
